name: Logic & Discrete Math
author: Recurse
subject: math
description: Truth tables, implications, sets, counting, proof techniques, and binary and modular arithmetic.

lesson.intro: Discrete math is the math of separate, countable things: true and false statements, sets, arrangements and whole numbers. It is the language of proofs and the foundation of computer science.

sections.title: Propositions and truth tables
sections.body:
A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. "7 is prime" is a proposition (true), and so is "10 is odd" (false). "Close the door" and "Is it raining?" are not propositions, and neither is "x > 3" until you know what x is.

Propositions combine with connectives:

- NOT P, written ¬P, is true when P is false
- P AND Q, written P ∧ Q, is true only when both are true
- P OR Q, written P ∨ Q, is true when at least one is true (an inclusive or)

A truth table lists every combination of truth values. With n variables there are 2ⁿ rows, because each new variable doubles the number of cases.

De Morgan's laws tell you how to negate AND and OR: negate each part and flip the connective.

- ¬(P ∧ Q) is the same as ¬P ∨ ¬Q
- ¬(P ∨ Q) is the same as ¬P ∧ ¬Q

"Not (hot and sunny)" means "not hot, or not sunny". In code, !(a && b) is the same as !a || !b.
sections.code:
P  Q | P ∧ Q | P ∨ Q | ¬P
T  T |   T   |   T   | F
T  F |   F   |   T   | F
F  T |   F   |   T   | T
F  F |   F   |   F   | T

check.question: When is P ∨ Q false?
choices: When exactly one of P and Q is true
Only when P and Q are both false
Only when P and Q are both true
Whenever P is false
check.explanation: Inclusive OR is true when at least one part is true, so its only false row is the one where both parts are false. "Exactly one is true" describes exclusive or, which is a different connective.

sections.title: Implication and the contrapositive
sections.body:
The implication P → Q reads "if P, then Q". P is the hypothesis and Q is the conclusion. It makes a promise only about cases where P is true, so it is false in exactly one case: P true and Q false. When P is false, the implication counts as true (vacuously true), because the promise was never tested.

From one implication you can build three related statements:

- Converse: Q → P
- Inverse: ¬P → ¬Q
- Contrapositive: ¬Q → ¬P

The contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original; the converse and inverse do not. Take "If it is a dog, then it is a mammal." The contrapositive, "If it is not a mammal, then it is not a dog," is equally true. The converse, "If it is a mammal, then it is a dog," is false: cats exist.

To negate an implication, describe the case that breaks it: the negation of P → Q is P ∧ ¬Q. The negation of "If you study, you pass" is "You study and you do not pass".
sections.code:
P  Q | P → Q
T  T |   T
T  F |   F     the only false row
F  T |   T
F  F |   T

check.question: What is the contrapositive of "If n is even, then n² is even"?
choices: If n² is even, then n is even
If n is not even, then n² is not even
n is even and n² is not even
If n² is not even, then n is not even
check.explanation: The contrapositive swaps the two parts and negates both: ¬Q → ¬P. "If n² is even, then n is even" is the converse, "If n is not even, then n² is not even" is the inverse, and "n is even and n² is not even" is the negation.

sections.title: Sets and counting
sections.body:
A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}.

- Union A ∪ B: elements in either set, {1, 2, 3, 4}
- Intersection A ∩ B: elements in both sets, {2, 3}
- Difference A − B: elements in A but not in B, {1}
- Subset: A ⊆ C means every element of A is also in C

To count a union, add the sizes and subtract the overlap you counted twice: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. Here 3 + 3 − 2 = 4.

Counting starts with the multiplication principle: if one choice has m options and a second has n, together there are m × n. Three shirts and four pairs of pants make 12 outfits.

For arrangements, the key question is whether order matters.

- Permutations (order matters): P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!
- Combinations (order does not matter): C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n − k)!)

Awarding gold, silver and bronze among 10 runners: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720 permutations. Choosing a 3-person committee from 10 people: each group of 3 appears 3! = 6 times among those 720 ordered lists, so C(10, 3) = 720 / 6 = 120.

check.question: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. What is A ∩ B?
check.explanation: The intersection keeps only elements that are in both sets: 3 and 4. {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is the union, and {1, 2} is A − B.

sections.title: Proof techniques
sections.body:
A proof is an argument that a statement must be true, with no exceptions. Checking examples is not enough: n² + n + 41 is prime for every n from 0 to 39, then fails at n = 40, where it equals 41². Three techniques cover most proofs.

Direct proof: assume the hypothesis and reason step by step to the conclusion. Claim: the sum of two even numbers is even. Write them as 2a and 2b. Their sum is 2a + 2b = 2(a + b), which is 2 times a whole number, so it is even.

Proof by contradiction: assume the statement is false and show that this leads to something impossible. Claim: √2 is irrational. Suppose √2 = p/q as a fraction in lowest terms. Then p² = 2q², so p² is even, so p is even; write p = 2k. Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k² and q is even too. But a fraction in lowest terms cannot have both parts even, so the assumption was wrong. (Proving the contrapositive, ¬Q → ¬P, is a close cousin of this method.)

Proof by induction proves a statement for every whole number n ≥ 1 in two parts:

- Base case: show it is true for n = 1
- Inductive step: assume it is true for n = k, and show it must then be true for n = k + 1

Think of a line of dominoes: the first one falls, and each one knocks over the next, so they all fall.
sections.code:
Claim: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2
Base (n = 1): 1 = 1·2/2   true
Step: assume 1 + ... + k = k(k + 1)/2
      1 + ... + k + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1)
                            = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2   which is the claim for k + 1

check.question: In a proof by induction, what does the inductive step show?
choices: The claim holds for n = 1
The claim holds for many tested values of n
If the claim holds for n = k, it also holds for n = k + 1
Assuming the claim is false leads to a contradiction
check.explanation: The inductive step is the link between neighbors: true for k forces true for k + 1. Showing the claim for n = 1 is the base case, and testing many values is not a proof at all.

sections.title: Binary and modular arithmetic
sections.body:
Binary is base 2. Each place is worth a power of 2 instead of a power of 10:

1011 in binary = 1·8 + 0·4 + 1·2 + 1·1 = 11

To convert a decimal number to binary, divide by 2 repeatedly and read the remainders from last to first. With n bits you can write 2ⁿ different values, from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1, so 8 bits cover 0 to 255.

Modular arithmetic is arithmetic with remainders. a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n: 17 mod 5 = 2, because 17 = 3·5 + 2. A clock works mod 12: 5 hours after 9 o'clock is 14 mod 12 = 2 o'clock. We write a ≡ b (mod n) when a and b leave the same remainder, for example 17 ≡ 2 (mod 5).

You can reduce at every step of an addition or multiplication, which keeps the numbers small. To find the last digit of 7⁴, work mod 10: 7² = 49 ≡ 9, and 9 × 9 = 81 ≡ 1, so 7⁴ ends in 1. (Indeed, 7⁴ = 2401.)
sections.code:
13 in binary:
13 ÷ 2 = 6  remainder 1
 6 ÷ 2 = 3  remainder 0
 3 ÷ 2 = 1  remainder 1
 1 ÷ 2 = 0  remainder 1
Read upward: 1101

check.question: What is 23 mod 7?
check.explanation: 23 = 3 × 7 + 2, so the remainder is 2. 3 is the quotient, not the remainder, and 16 is 23 − 7, which takes away only one 7.

keyTerms.definition: A statement that is either true or false.
¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q: to negate, negate each part and flip AND and OR.
For P → Q, the statement ¬Q → ¬P, which is always logically equivalent to the original.
An arrangement where order matters; P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!.
A selection where order does not matter; C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n − k)!).
Assuming a statement is false and deriving something impossible, which shows the statement is true.
Proving a base case and that truth for k implies truth for k + 1, which proves a claim for every n.
Arithmetic on remainders; a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n.

summary: P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false; its contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P is equivalent, but its converse is not.
De Morgan's laws: to negate AND or OR, negate each part and flip the connective.
Use permutations when order matters and combinations when it does not: C(n, k) = P(n, k) / k!.
Induction needs both a base case and an inductive step; contradiction assumes the opposite and reaches an impossibility.
Binary places are powers of 2, and a mod n is the remainder after dividing a by n.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why "if it is not a mammal, it is not a dog" says exactly the same thing as "if it is a dog, it is a mammal", while "if it is a mammal, it is a dog" does not.

questions.question: Which statement is equivalent to ¬(P ∧ Q)?
choices: ¬P ∨ ¬Q
¬P ∧ ¬Q
P ∨ Q
¬P ∧ Q
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law: negating an AND gives an OR of the negations. ¬P ∧ ¬Q is too strong; it claims both are false, while ¬(P ∧ Q) only says they are not both true. With P true and Q false, ¬(P ∧ Q) is true but ¬P ∧ ¬Q is false.

questions.question: A rule says: deny entry if NOT (age ≥ 18 OR has a permit). Which condition is equivalent?
choices: age < 18 OR no permit
age ≤ 18 AND no permit
age < 18 AND has a permit
age < 18 AND no permit
questions.explanation: By De Morgan, NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). NOT (age ≥ 18) is age < 18, and NOT (has a permit) is no permit. age ≤ 18 would wrongly deny 18-year-olds.

questions.question: When is the implication P → Q false?
choices: When P is false and Q is true
When P is true and Q is false
When P and Q are both false
Whenever Q is false
questions.explanation: An implication only breaks its promise when the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. If P is false, the implication is vacuously true. "Whenever Q is false" misses that the row with P false and Q false is true.

questions.question: "If a shape is a square, then it is a rectangle" is true. Which statement must also be true?
choices: If a shape is a rectangle, then it is a square
If a shape is not a rectangle, then it is not a square
If a shape is not a square, then it is not a rectangle
Some squares are not rectangles
questions.explanation: The contrapositive (not a rectangle → not a square) is always equivalent to the original. The converse (rectangle → square) fails for a 2 × 5 rectangle, and so does the inverse (not a square → not a rectangle).

questions.question: Why is "if P, then Q" counted as true when P is false?
questions.answer: The implication only promises something about cases where P is true. When P is false the promise is never tested, so it cannot have been broken; the statement is vacuously true.
questions.explanation: "If you score 100, I will buy you lunch" is not a lie if you score 80 and get no lunch. Only scoring 100 and getting no lunch breaks it, which matches the single false row of the truth table.

questions.question: What is the negation of "If it rains, the game is cancelled"?
choices: If it does not rain, the game is not cancelled
If it rains, the game is not cancelled
It does not rain and the game is cancelled
It rains and the game is not cancelled
questions.explanation: The negation of P → Q is P ∧ ¬Q, the one situation that makes the original false. "If it rains, the game is not cancelled" is just another implication; on a dry day both it and the original are vacuously true, so it cannot be the negation.

questions.question: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and B = {4, 5, 6, 7}. How many elements are in A ∪ B?
questions.explanation: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| = 5 + 4 − 2 = 7. The union is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. Answering 9 counts 4 and 5 twice.

questions.question: In how many ways can gold, silver and bronze medals be awarded among 8 runners?
questions.explanation: Order matters, so this is a permutation: 8 choices for gold, then 7 for silver, then 6 for bronze: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. C(8, 3) = 56 would treat the three medals as identical.

questions.question: In how many ways can a 3-person committee be chosen from 8 people?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter: C(8, 3) = (8 × 7 × 6) / 3! = 336 / 6 = 56. Each committee appears 6 times among the 336 ordered lists, so divide by 6.

questions.question: Which situation calls for combinations rather than permutations?
choices: Choosing 5 cards for a poker hand
Setting a 4-digit PIN with no repeated digits
Ranking the top 3 finishers in a race
Electing a president, a treasurer and a secretary
questions.explanation: A poker hand is the same hand in any order, so you count combinations. A PIN, a ranking and distinct officer roles all change when the order changes, so they are permutations.

questions.question: To prove √2 is irrational, you suppose √2 = p/q in lowest terms and show p and q must both be even. Which technique is this?
choices: Direct proof
Proof by induction
Proof by contradiction
Proof by cases
questions.explanation: You assume the opposite of the claim (that √2 is rational) and reach an impossibility (a fraction in lowest terms with both parts even). That is proof by contradiction. A direct proof would start from the hypothesis and argue forward to the claim.

questions.question: An induction argument shows that "true for n = k" implies "true for n = k + 1", but never checks a base case. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; the inductive step alone proves the claim
The claim is then proved only for even n
Nothing has been shown true, so the chain never starts
The claim is proved for every n except n = 1
questions.explanation: The inductive step only says each domino knocks over the next; without a base case, no domino ever falls. The false claim "n = n + 1" has a valid inductive step (add 1 to both sides) but no true base case.

questions.question: What is the difference between a direct proof and a proof by contradiction?
questions.answer: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and reasons forward to the conclusion. A proof by contradiction assumes the conclusion is false and shows this leads to something impossible, so the conclusion must be true.
questions.explanation: Direct: 2a + 2b = 2(a + b) shows the sum of two evens is even. Contradiction suits claims like "√2 is irrational" or "there are infinitely many primes", where assuming the opposite gives you something concrete to work with.

questions.question: What is the binary number 101101 in decimal?
questions.explanation: Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The 1s sit at 32, 8, 4 and 1, so the value is 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.

questions.question: Write 25 in binary.
questions.explanation: 25 = 16 + 8 + 1. The places 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 get the digits 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, so 25 is 11001. Repeated division by 2 gives remainders 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, which read upward give the same answer.

questions.question: It is 10 o'clock. What hour will a 12-hour clock show 30 hours later?
questions.explanation: 10 + 30 = 40, and 40 mod 12 = 4 because 40 = 3 × 12 + 4. The clock shows 4 o'clock.

questions.question: What is the last digit of 3¹⁰⁰?
questions.explanation: Work mod 10. The last digits of powers of 3 repeat every 4 steps: 3, 9, 7, 1, 3, 9, ... Since 100 mod 4 = 0, 3¹⁰⁰ ends the same way as 3⁴ = 81, in 1.
